item.title: Clustered heatmaps in Python with canvasxpress
item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
The clustered heatmap is the default way to look at an expression matrix: rows and columns reordered by similarity, dendrograms on the margins, and sample metadata alongside. Here we build one in Python with canvasxpress — clustering happens inside the render, so you pass a plain matrix and get an interactive, reproducible figure.

Install

pip install canvasxpress

An expression matrix with sample metadata

Swap this simulated block for your own matrix (genes in rows, samples in columns) and a table of per-sample annotations.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng   = np.random.default_rng(1)
ng, ns = 40, 30
genes = [f"Gene{i+1}" for i in range(ng)]
samps = [f"S{i+1}"    for i in range(ns)]
cond  = ["Tumor"] * (ns // 2) + ["Normal"] * (ns // 2)

m = rng.normal(0, 1, (ng, ns))
tumor = [i for i, c in enumerate(cond) if c == "Tumor"]
normal = [i for i, c in enumerate(cond) if c == "Normal"]
m[np.ix_(range(0, 20),  tumor)]  += 2      # first block up in Tumor
m[np.ix_(range(20, 40), normal)] += 2      # second block up in Normal

expr = pd.DataFrame(m.round(3), index=genes, columns=samps)

Build the spec

The matrix goes in as data, and the sample annotation becomes an annotation track over the columns. samplesClustered / variablesClustered turn on hierarchical clustering with dendrograms.

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

data = {
    "y": {"vars": genes, "smps": samps, "data": expr.values.tolist()},
    "x": {"Condition": cond},
}

config = {
    "graphType": "Heatmap",
    "samplesClustered": True, "variablesClustered": True,
    "colorSpectrum": ["navy", "white", "firebrick3"],
    "showSmpDendrogram": True, "showVarDendrogram": True,
    "title": "Clustered expression heatmap",
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="heatmap", data=data, config=config, width=650, height=550)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)

Rows and columns are reordered by similarity, the dendrograms show the clustering, and the samples separate cleanly by condition. Hover a cell for its gene, sample and value; the whole figure is one portable spec you can store, validate and re-render from R or JavaScript.

item.title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in Python with canvasxpress
item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
Kaplan–Meier curves summarize time-to-event data: the step-down survival probability over time, usually split by a group like treatment arm. Here we build one in Python with canvasxpress — it computes the survival steps for you from a time column and a censoring column — and the result is interactive and reproducible.

Install

pip install canvasxpress

A survival table

Swap this simulated block for your own data: per subject you need a follow-up time, a censoring indicator (1 = censored, 0 = event), and the grouping variable.

import numpy as np

rng  = np.random.default_rng(1)
n    = 200
arm  = rng.choice(["Treatment", "Control"], n)
base = np.where(arm == "Treatment", 60, 40)     # treatment survives longer
time = np.round(rng.exponential(base), 1)
cens = rng.binomial(1, 0.3, n)                  # 1 = censored, 0 = event
subj = [f"Subj{i+1}" for i in range(n)]

Build the spec

The two columns — the time and its matching censor flag — go in as the variable samples, and the arm rides along as a variable annotation. The key is graphType="KaplanMeier" and passing both columns to xAxis.

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

data = {
    # Subjects are the variables (rows); each row holds [Time, Time-Censor].
    "y": {"vars": subj, "smps": ["Time", "Time-Censor"],
          "data": [[t, c] for t, c in zip(time.tolist(), cens.tolist())]},
    "z": {"Arm": arm.tolist()},
}

config = {
    "graphType": "KaplanMeier",
    "xAxis": ["Time", "Time-Censor"],
    "colorBy": "Arm",
    "title": "Overall survival by treatment arm",
    "xAxisTitle": "Time (weeks)", "yAxisTitle": "Probability of survival",
    "invertCensored": True,               # draw censoring ticks
    "showKMConfidenceIntervals": False,
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="km", data=data, config=config, width=650, height=500)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)

Hover any step for the time and survival probability; the tick marks are censored subjects. canvasxpress derives the survival curve from the raw table, so you never precompute the steps — and the same spec re-renders the identical curve from R or JavaScript.

A common gotcha

The survival transform only fires with graphType="KaplanMeier". A bare "Scatter2D" gives a raw scatter of the censor values instead — survival probability is computed by the engine, not a column in your data.

item.title: Interactive volcano plots in Python with canvasxpress
item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
A volcano plot is the workhorse of differential-expression analysis: log fold change on x, statistical significance on y, and the interesting genes pushed to the top corners. Here we build one in Python with canvasxpress — interactive (zoom, hover, filter) and reproducible: the whole figure is one portable specification you can store and re-render from Python, R or JavaScript.

Install

pip install canvasxpress

A differential-expression table

Swap this simulated block for your own results — the output of any DE pipeline works, as long as you have a log fold change and a significance value per gene.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import norm

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 1000
genes = [f"Gene{i+1}" for i in range(n)]

# Simulate a realistic volcano: most genes have no real effect, a minority are
# differentially expressed. Significance follows effect size / standard error, which
# is what gives a volcano its shape.
de     = rng.random(n) < 0.12                              # ~12% truly changed
sign   = rng.choice([-1, 1], n)
effect = np.where(de, sign * (0.8 + 0.9 * rng.random(n)), 0.0)   # true log2FC
se     = 0.22 + 0.5 * rng.random(n)                        # per-gene standard error
logfc  = effect + rng.normal(0, se)                        # observed log2FC
pval   = 2 * norm.sf(np.abs(logfc / se))                   # z-test p-value
neglogp = np.minimum(-np.log10(pval), 16)

df = pd.DataFrame({"logFC": logfc.round(3), "-log-pVal": neglogp.round(3)}, index=genes)

def classify(fc, p):
    if fc > 1 and p > 1.3:   return "Increased"
    if fc < -1 and p > 1.3:  return "Decreased"
    return "NoChange"

group = [classify(fc, p) for fc, p in zip(df["logFC"], df["-log-pVal"])]
fold  = (2 ** df["logFC"].abs()).round(2)

Build the spec

canvasxpress takes a data object (a value matrix plus annotations) and a config. We put the two measurements as the variable’s samples and carry the regulation call and fold change as variable annotations (z).

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

data = {
    # Genes are the variables (rows); each row holds [logFC, -log-pVal].
    "y": {"vars": genes, "smps": ["logFC", "-log-pVal"],
          "data": [[fc, p] for fc, p in zip(df["logFC"], df["-log-pVal"])]},
    "z": {"Group": group, "FC": fold.tolist()},
}

config = {
    "graphType": "Scatter2D",
    "title": "Publication-ready volcano plot",
    "xAxis": ["logFC"], "yAxis": ["-log-pVal"],
    "xAxisTitle": "log2 fold change", "yAxisTitle": "-log10 p-value",
    "colorBy": "Group",
    "colorKey": {"Group": {"Increased": "rgba(197,27,38,0.75)",
                            "Decreased": "rgba(33,102,172,0.75)",
                            "NoChange":  "rgba(150,150,150,0.35)"}},
    "sizeBy": "FC", "sizes": [3, 6, 9, 12, 15],
    "showDecorations": True,
    "decorations": {"line": [
        {"color": "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", "width": 1, "x": 1},
        {"color": "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", "width": 1, "x": -1},
        {"color": "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", "width": 1, "y": 1.301},
    ]},
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="volcano", data=data, config=config, width=650, height=500)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)

The chart is interactive — hover a point for its gene and values, drag to zoom, filter by regulation group in the toolbar. The dashed guides mark the ±1 log2FC and p = 0.05 cutoffs.

Why “reproducible”

Everything above serializes to one JSON specification — the data and the config. That spec is portable: the identical figure renders from the R (canvasXpress) and JavaScript packages, and it can be validated against a published schema and re-rendered later, so a figure in a paper can be regenerated and audited rather than just viewed.
